The Tiber River. The river on which Rome was founded and grew into the capital of the ancient Mediterranean world. Flowing two hundred and fifty-two miles from the Apennine Mountains through central Italy to the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Tiber was Rome's lifeline for trade, defense, and agriculture.

The Tiber originates in the Apennine Mountains and flows through Tuscany and central Italy before reaching Rome and emptying into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Rome's position at a shallow ford of the Tiber made it a natural crossroads for trade between the Mediterranean and the interior of Italy. The Tiber provided Rome with water, fish, and grain from its flood plain. The river's valley was fertile and agriculturally rich, supporting the growing city.

Roman legend traces the city's founding to seven fifty-three BCE and attributes Romulus and Remus's rescue to the Tiber's banks, where a she-wolf found and raised the two brothers. The Tiber was notoriously prone to flooding. Severe floods were often interpreted as divine omens and attributed to the gods' displeasure at human behavior. Popes and medieval Rome built bridges and ports along the Tiber, and the river remained Rome's lifeline even after the empire's fall into history.

The Tiber is inseparable from Rome's founding, growth, and identity as a civilization. The river supported Rome's early expansion and trade throughout the Mediterranean world. Rome's rise to world dominion depended entirely on the Tiber's resources and the access it provided. Roman legend places the brothers Romulus and Remus on the Tiber's banks, and this river was central to central Italian geography and history throughout the ages, remaining sacred to Rome even today.
